findings.why: The scenario stem sets two goals -- records 'intact AND reachable' -- and then the task line asks only for AVAILABILITY. A candidate who anchors on the scenario has a defensible reason to select 'Digital signatures on lab results' (the only control that keeps records 'intact'), and the same pull inflates confidence in 'Offline immutable backups' for the wrong reason. The stem and the selection rule point at different buckets.
findings.suggested_fix: Drop 'intact and' from the scenario, or restate the task as 'protects the REACHABILITY of records (availability) rather than their correctness'.

findings.why: This is a depth-7 site whose items are strictly easier than its own module gate: the gate uses full scenario sentences ('Requiring a password plus a one-time code from the user's phone'), while this d7 bank uses bare canonical noun phrases ('An iris scan', 'A registered fingerprint') that are the textbook definition examples for each factor. Every item is answerable by dictionary recall with no discrimination between a candidate who understands factor independence and one who memorised the three examples. Passing d7 adds no evidence beyond the gate.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the canonical noun phrases with items that stress factor boundaries -- e.g. 'A push approval you tap in an app you are already logged into', 'A recovery code printed and kept in your wallet', 'Your typing rhythm measured during login' -- and keep at least one item where the naive surface cue is wrong.

buckets_in_tension: Canon II — act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
Canon I — protect society and the infrastructure
Canon III — provide diligent and competent service to principals
Canon IV — advance and protect the profession
findings.why: Canon II ('act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally') is a superset bucket: every other item in the bank is also an instance of acting honourably/responsibly -- reporting a dispatch-system flaw (I), declining work you are not qualified for (III), reporting a peer selling leaked exam material (IV). Nothing in the bucket labels tells the candidate that Canon II is meant to be the residual bucket used only when no more specific canon applies, so a defensible reading collapses several items into II.
findings.suggested_fix: State the disambiguation rule in the prompt ('assign to the most specific canon; use Canon II only where no other canon governs'), and keep Canon II items where the specific canons plainly do not reach.

findings.item: A client pressures you to overstate their security posture in an audit report, and you refuse
buckets_in_tension: Canon II — act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
Canon III — provide diligent and competent service to principals
findings.why: Refusing to falsify an audit report is Canon II (truthful, objective reporting), but the item is framed entirely as a duty owed to a named principal -- 'A client pressures you...' -- and Canon III is literally the canon about service to principals ('respect their trust and the privileges they grant you'). Two of the three 'client' items in this bank key to Canon III, so the surface cue 'client -> principals -> Canon III' is reinforced by the bank itself and misfires exactly here. A candidate who has learned the canon-to-item mapping by the principal/public/profession axis lands on III with a real argument.
findings.suggested_fix: Remove the principal framing from the stem -- e.g. 'You refuse to sign off an audit report that overstates the security posture' -- or move the item to a bank that does not also contain two client-facing Canon III items.

findings.item: Safeguarding client information is a responsibility of every employee, at every level
findings.why: This item and 'The organisation will protect the confidentiality of all customer data' are the same artefact type expressed twice: both are broad, non-measurable statements of organisational intent, i.e. Policy. Because the bank presents 5 buckets over 8 items, a candidate reasonably infers the two near-identical statements are meant to be discriminated and pushes one of them into Standard -- and no wording in either item supports the split (neither names a technology, a threshold, or a mandatory configuration).
findings.suggested_fix: Keep one policy statement and convert the other into a genuine standard with a measurable mandate (e.g. 'Client information must be labelled and stored only in the approved managed repository'), or reduce to one item per artefact type.

findings.why: This item is a restatement of the module gate item 'Background checks run before a new hire starts', with the same key (administrative). The d7 constructset is supposed to demonstrate depth beyond the gate, but for this item it re-tests the identical construct with identical wording modulo tense, so a correct response is evidence of nothing new and inflates the d7 pass rate.
findings.suggested_fix: Swap in an administrative control not already used at the gate that is harder to place -- e.g. 'A documented exception-approval workflow for firewall rule changes' or 'Mandatory annual re-certification of user access rights'.

findings.why: The keyed answer is Availability (data is unreachable), but attacker-side encryption is also an unauthorised modification of stored data, so Integrity is arguable, and the surface word 'encrypts' pulls naive candidates toward Confidentiality. The item is still answerable because the bank's other Availability item is a pure flooding attack and the Integrity items are explicit modifications, so a well-prepared candidate resolves it.
findings.suggested_fix: Say what the victim experiences rather than what the attacker does: 'Ransomware leaves the file server's data unusable until a ransom is paid.'

findings.why: 'Immutable' is an integrity property, so the item can be read as primarily integrity-protecting; 'primarily' plus the ransomware-recovery scenario resolves it to availability, but the word choice fights the key.
findings.suggested_fix: Use 'Offline backups held on write-protected media' or simply 'Offline backup copies kept out of band'.

findings.item: You report a peer who is selling leaked ISC2 exam questions to candidates
buckets_in_tension: Canon IV — advance and protect the profession
Canon II — act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
findings.why: Reporting a peer who sells leaked exam content protects the certification and hence the profession (Canon IV), but the peer's conduct is an illegal breach of the ISC2 agreement, and Canon II's guidance ('observe all contracts and agreements') gives a candidate a route to II. IV remains the stronger reading because the harm is to the credential rather than to any party you serve.
findings.suggested_fix: Sharpen the profession framing: 'You report a peer who is devaluing the certification by selling leaked ISC2 exam questions.'

findings.item: You tell a client up front that a specialised cloud engagement is beyond what you are qualified to deliver
buckets_in_tension: Canon III — provide diligent and competent service to principals
findings.why: 'beyond what you are qualified to deliver' is a near-synonym of the bucket label's 'competent service', so the item can be answered by lexical matching without knowing that scope-of-competence sits under the duty to principals.
findings.suggested_fix: Rephrase without the competence vocabulary: 'You tell a client up front that you have never delivered a cloud engagement of this type before they sign.'

findings.item: Separation of duties on payment approvals
findings.why: Separation of duties is an administrative/managerial control by intent, but on a payment-approval system it is normally enforced by application configuration, so a candidate who classifies by implementation rather than by origin can defend OUT. 'Safeguard on the plan' framing favours the administrative reading.
findings.suggested_fix: Anchor it as policy: 'A policy requiring two different named approvers for every payment'.
